text: Getting an accurate read on grain quality or moisture starts with taking a fair, representative sample rather than checking only what is easiest to reach (for example, only the top surface of a pile or the first bag off a truck). The source describes slightly different sampling techniques depending on where the grain sits: sampling standing rice in the field before harvest; sampling grain already in a storage bin, which involves drawing smaller sub-samples from several depths and positions inside the bin and combining them into one composite sample rather than scooping from a single spot; sampling bagged grain, typically using a grain probe/trier inserted into a number of different bags and positions rather than relying on one bag; and sampling a truck or vehicle load of grain being delivered or loaded, which should be drawn from multiple points as the grain is moved rather than just the visible top layer, since deliveries can be deliberately or accidentally uneven in quality. For moisture content specifically, the source gives the standard oven-drying style formula: moisture percentage equals (weight before drying minus weight after drying) divided by weight before drying, multiplied by 100. The source also illustrates a simple rule-of-thumb approach for choosing how many individual bags or units to inspect out of a larger lot — roughly using the square root of the lot size as a practical sample count for a quick check (for example, checking about 3 units out of a lot of 9, or about 10 out of a lot of 100) — which is meant as a fast field shortcut rather than a substitute for formal statistical sampling. For any transaction where money changes hands based on grain quality or moisture (buying/selling paddy, seed certification, etc.), it is worth using a proper moisture meter and following a consistent sampling method rather than relying on visual judgment or a single spot-check. (Note: the sampling and sample-size guidance here is simplified from the source's illustrative examples; for formal grading or certification purposes, follow the specific procedure required by the buyer, mill, or certification body involved.)
